Industry News: This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

In a recent development, it included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

In a recent development, for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

Recent findings suggest that from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

Sources indicate that the average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own indicated modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Sources indicate that several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, stated that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

Recent findings suggest that “Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” noted Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

In a recent development, theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he stated.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” remarked Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

Industry observers note that “Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he remarked. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

Sources indicate that “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being key,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

In a recent development, first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the upcoming Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

According to recent reports, compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

According to recent reports, as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

In a recent development, over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the tech giant has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

In a recent development, the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

In a recent development, to ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

Why Better Recovery Might Be the Missing Link in Your Workout Routine

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • It has been revealed that you work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps.
  • According to recent reports, A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that you work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps. But no matter what you do lately, it seems as if your progress just won’t budge. So what’s going on?

According to recent reports, A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking. The solution for your stall in progress may lie in something a little simpler: recovery.

Industry observers note that many people think results happen during our sweat sessions, but in actuality, the gains we’re working toward happen afterward. Adapting to stress, building muscle, and getting stronger all happen when we take rest. So, before you fire your personal trainer or scour the internet for a upcoming workout plan, try making a few simple tweaks to how you spend your downtime, if you’re even giving yourself any.

Read on for what the science and experts say about recovery—and how you can use yours to escape your fitness plateau.

Meet the experts: Donna Duffy, PhD, is an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro, and head of research at Collective X Health, a women's health intelligence and research platform co-founded by WH advisory board member Stacy Sims. Lisa Woodroffe, MD, is a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. Asad Siddiqi, DO, is the chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital.

Working out is only one piece of the equation when it comes to seeing results. In order to get all the benefits of training, your body needs time to rest and recover after a workout. “During rest, your body recovers using sleep, food, and downtime to repair the tissues you’ve stressed during training and prepare them to handle the next challenge,” indicates Donna Duffy, PhD, an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot that goes on in your body during rest: In addition to your muscles repairing and building back stronger, you experience a nervous system reset—as your heart rate decreases after a training session, your body shifts out of a stressed state and begins to calm down, Duffy explains. Then there is increased blood flow during and after exercise, which helps flush out things like lactic acid and delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to stressed parts of the body.

That is, assuming you’re giving your body enough time to do all that. “If you continually pile more workouts on top of fatigue without giving your body enough time and resources to recover, that fatigue can start to interfere with your overall performance in and out of the gym,” Duffy says.

When a person fails to recover adequately, a weight that seemed doable on Monday feels heavier on Wednesday, and an easy run becomes a hard one. All of this can be incredibly frustrating, and may make people think they just need to work harder, but experts say sometimes the opposite is true. “Your body may not need more training,” notes Duffy. “Instead, it may need more opportunity to recover from the training you're already doing.”.

Your body may be sending you signals that you’re not as well recovered as you think. According to Duffy, some common signs that your body has not recovered well include:.

Industry observers note that showing signs of poor recovery? Start by making these tweaks.

When deciding if your body needs a rest, consider factors like workout duration, intensity, and fatigue, indicates Asad Siddiqi, DO, chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital. Soreness or fatigue that stays below a 3 to 4 out of 10 during or immediately after training and does not last beyond 24 to 36 hours is the upper limit of “acceptable” exercise-induced discomfort, and a day in between loading is probably fine. Meanwhile, if you go above a 5, Dr. Siddiqi recommends taking an extra day beyond that to monitor how you’re recovering before doing the same workout again. Typically, a two-day break will allow people enough time to recover, but the most vital barometer is how you feel, he says. If you’re still super sore and think your form will be compromised, you need more time off.

Bob and Brad A7 Pro Massage Gun with Heat and Cold Therapy.

TriggerPoint Grid Multi-Density Foam Roller.

This doesn’t mean you need to be completely inactive during those days off, particularly if you’re doing circuit training. If you hit arms really hard on Monday and need to give them some extra time to recover, you can still do legs the next day. But, if you are doing intense and fatiguing full-body workouts, try alternating resistance training with low-impact aerobic or mobility exercises like yoga.

According to recent reports, even if you’re doing circuit training, at a minimum, most people should have at least one full rest day per week, indicates Lisa Woodroffe, MD, a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. And, if you’re someone who has been feeling consistently sore, unusually fatigued, or seeing a dip in performance, it’s time to up your number of rest days.

Sources indicate that for a variety of reasons, many active people are just simply not eating enough, says Dr. Woodroffe. “They are either underestimating how much energy they are expending in exercise, or overestimating what they are eating, or with busy schedules running out of time in their day to get everything they need.” It’s also worth mentioning that some people may be exercising with the explicit goal of losing weight—which can result in underfueling for their workouts, she says.

In a recent development, eating enough is critical for recovery. “We know that insufficient fueling patterns have cascading and multiplying effects on the body’s ability to respond to training load and recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe indicates. “All cells of the body need adequate energy to maintain optimal function. When there is not enough energy to go around, there will be effects not only at the cellular level but eventually also at the organ system level.” We’re talking effects on muscle recovery, bone density, cardiovascular function, and cognitive performance.

That’s why experts recommend having a blueprint in place for getting all the fuel you need. “Emphasizing a routine of three to five meals a day that includes carbs for energy, protein for muscle building, and fresh vegetables and fruits for minerals and gut health is the baseline,” notes Dr. Siddiqi. You don’t need to count calories if that’s not your thing—but you should have a goal of at least three meals supplemented by additional snacks every day that hit all of the macros (carbs, protein, and fats).

It has been revealed that protein is particularly vital for active people, but no macro should be ignored. Dr. Woodroffe always notes that no food groups should be restricted unless otherwise directed by a medical professional. If you need any help with your fueling strategy, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor or dietitian who can give you personalized recommendations.

One overall, simple way to make sure you’re eating enough? Feeling full. You should eat to be satiated and not feel constantly hungry. When it comes to snacking, it’s recommended that you eat easily digestible carbs (Think: fruit, bagels, toast) 30 to 60 minutes before a workout, and then a combination of carbs, protein, and fluids within 60 minutes following. It’s one reason dietitians love chocolate milk as a post-workout drink.

Your training program is a balancing act. “A plateau can happen either due to not enough training, or not enough recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe states. But how can we actually tell which one is happening? What are the clues that someone needs to pull back versus increase the challenge?

“Overall, training should be a positive experience that challenges the body and mind but doesn’t put you out of commission,” Dr. Siddiqi says. You want to be sore after a workout, but not so much that you can’t move. If you’re experiencing the symptoms above that are signs you’re not recovering properly, you’re probably overloading and should pull back. Start by taking two full rest days to give your body a real chance to recover, and then consider implementing one additional rest day per week compared to your old schedule or adjusting your training plan to allow for less intensity.

On the flip side, if you’re plateauing and not feeling drained at all, then it may be because you need to challenge yourself more. If that’s the case, Dr. Siddiqi recommends a steady increase in load by roughly 10 percent week over week. “The definition of ‘load’ in this situation is variable, and so this could mean 10 percent more intense based on your perceived exertion, 10 percent greater distance, 10 percent greater duration, or however else you think could be meaningful,” he says. The key, though, is to have a steady increase on your way to your goal, avoiding any major spikes.

It has been revealed that so how do you know when symptoms are more than just poor recovery after a challenging workout versus a health issue that needs a professional follow-up? “Sometimes fatigue, soreness, or a dip in performance really can be a sign that you need more recovery, but it's also key not to assume that every change is caused by your training,” says Duffy. “If symptoms are persistent, getting worse, or affecting your ability to function normally, there may be something else going on.”.

Duffy suggests seeing a health care professional if:.

Whatever you may be experiencing—a regular old case of doing too much or something more serious—consider this your sign to take a second, check in with yourself, and don’t hesitate to ask for support. You’ll be out there moving again (and even better) before you know it.

#75753. Breaking: The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1506 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed.
  • Sources indicate that until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon.
  • “To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed. Sure, I might not have bulging muscles—but I confess I occasionally survey the other men in the gym and entertain the idea that I might be the hottest guy in the room. Sometimes, though, a bigger, better looking dude walks in and starts lifting heavier weights than me. My confidence evaporates, along with, I imagine, the admiring glances of all the men and women (who, on reflection, might not actually have been paying me any mind).

Sources indicate that until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon. Mogging, derived from “alpha Male Of the Group,” describes the act of one man outshining another, through any combination of height, muscularity, facial attractiveness, status, or charisma (a.k.a. “aura”). On the receiving end, it’s the sudden, visceral realization that another man might be stronger or better-looking than you, and the cascade of feelings of inferiority that follow.

“To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular. The 20-year-old looksmaxxing influencer was spectacularly “frame-mogged” on his own livestream in a viral moment earlier this year. The curious phrasing captured online attention, and on November 3 “mogging” was crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2026.

But this type of social scenario didn’t just emerge with the dawn of the internet. I was curious: Does this emasculating sensation stem from an ancient status instinct, an ego threat, a form of social comparison, or something else? And why are some men so sensitive to it?

THIS ISSUE OF mogging raises a question: Why should another man’s stature have such an immediate effect on my self-esteem? It’s a theme explored in the classics. In Homer’s Iliad, the ancient Greek epic, King Priam spots the enormous warrior Ajax, “whose head and shoulders tower above the rest.” Yet Homer also understood that size wasn't everything. Earlier in the same passage, Menelaus is described as broader-shouldered than Odysseus, the cunning hero played by Matt Damon in The Odyssey—but the shorter man’s extraordinary eloquence renders his stature irrelevant.

Industry observers note that modern researchers have also looked for answers. Human judgment “is by nature comparative” and social comparisons are “spontaneous, effortless, and unintentional reactions to the performance of others,” according to a 2014 review of the early indications on the brain mechanisms of social comparison and their influence on the reward system.

Meanwhile, other related research found that physically stronger men were perceived as having higher social status, partly because they were considered more capable leaders. But does this make the discomfort of being mogged inevitable?

Psychologists distinguish between dominance, in which status is secured through intimidation, and prestige, which is earned through the admiration of others. Research suggests that even if the strongest and most attractive may initially draw outsized attention, or mog, prestige is ultimately conferred upon those who benefit the group, rather than pursue aggressive self-interest.

For couples therapist Sarah Tilley, this dynamic reflects the tension between our instinctive deference to appearances and our recognition of its limitations. Snap judgments of competence from candidates’ faces predicted almost 69 percent of US senate races in 2004, according to a study in Science,.

“There is a deference to beauty and we’re all culprits,” she states. “Beauty trumps intelligence, but only for a short amount of time. Smart people will know that, but it takes wisdom.” In other words, the actual effects of a mog could be fleeting if there is someone smarter in the room.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY happening when you feel the mog? Turns out, there are chemical responses behind those feelings of self-doubt.

“A review of more than 200 lab studies found that our cortisol is reliably spiked when we feel that others are judging us and when we can’t control the outcome,” notes Dr Manesh Girn, a neuroscientist and men’s work facilitator.

“Envy toward someone who outranks you on something you care about also activates the anterior cingulate cortex, a region tied to processing pain and conflict,” he says, citing a study on the neural correlates of envy and schadenfreude (the feeling of satisfaction when someone faces consequences they deserve).

In a recent development, but the susceptibility to feeling mogged also depends on one’s values and sense of self-worth. “Shorter men are more sensitive than taller men to dominance cues in other men's faces and voices,” adds Girn. In the envy study, pain responses only arose when the other person’s perceived superiority was in a domain the participant particularly cared about.

In a recent development, looksmaxxer-in-chief Peters admitted last month that he now simply removes himself from social settings when there’s a possibility he might be mogged. “It really has a soul-crushing effect,” he told podcaster Patrick Bet-David, recalling a recent weight room encounter. “We just felt the mog from all the way across the gym to the point where I just left. Why would I want that internal pressure?”.

Such an extreme reaction suggests “a maladaptive mindset,” claims Charlotte Markey, a professor of psychology at Rutgers University. “Social comparison is a very normal process, including in terms of our physical attributes.”.

For some men in 2026, that drives an obsession to become the strongest of the pack. This can become genuinely debilitating.

In a recent development, “I've cared for young people who then go to the gym five plus hours a day, and it starts to detract from their quality of life,” claims Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, who researches male body image. “The concern is when self-improvement becomes self-worth, because it becomes dependent on outperforming someone else.”.

Industry observers note that and while this might be driven by instinct, the experts caution against succumbing to our baser instincts. “It may be evolutionarily baked in,” says Markey, “but we want to be careful not to oversimplify here. We aren’t cavemen.”.

Industry observers note that HOWEVER, THE CAVEMAN is not quite dead. We form impressions of a face within a tenth of a second, and people can estimate a man’s upper body strength from his face alone. For our ancestors, misjudging who could beat them in a fight may have been a costly mistake. Some research suggests that our sensitivity to physical formidability reflects this ancient pressure, which may help explain why strength continues to influence perceptions of status.

Recent findings suggest that despite sometimes feeling the mog (and after injuries that prevent heavy lifting), I’m generally content to stick to lighter weights in the gym rather than packing on mass to stand out more in a room. Yet I wonder whether my own instinctive competitiveness has affected my relationships with other men. If I’m constantly assessing where I stand in some invisible hierarchy, like a dog jostling for position in its pack, surely it becomes more difficult to strike up friendships.

In a recent development, in a 2017 study of 100 physically active young men, researchers found that those at risk of muscle dysmorphia were less inclined to socialize than their peers, potentially due to social comparison tendencies. The pursuit of the perfect physique, it seems, can come at the expense of the very relationships it might be intended to improve.

Recent findings suggest that SO WHY, AFTER millennia of social comparison, do we have this very modern understanding of the mogging dynamic? Social media has transformed what was once a largely local competition into a global one, exposing men to an endless parade of gorgeous bodies and faces against which to measure themselves (albeit at lower rates than women). “The Greeks didn’t compare themselves with the best, idealized versions of everyone in the world,” notes Nagata.

Indeed, researchers effectively recreated the experience of being mogged in a study involving 300 men aged 18 to 30. They were randomly assigned to view images of bare-chested and muscular men alongside clothed photos and pictures of scenery. Exposure to the half-naked Chads resulted in significantly lower body satisfaction.

According to recent reports, I would never flee a gym or a bar upon the entrance of a potentially more attractive man. But back in April—shortly after mogging entered my lexicon—I couldn’t help noticing how much attention a very handsome (and very muscular) longtime male friend was receiving. One woman I didn’t even know basically cat-called him on the street and complimented his outfit. Naturally I assessed my own. It wasn’t nearly as cool, I lamented.

Recent findings suggest that now, after years of feeling this mysterious, disempowering sensation in his organization without entirely being able to place it, I had a name for my predicament: I’d been mogged. Still, I was able to keep it together. We enjoyed our lunch, and we remain friends.

Perhaps the instinct to compare ourselves is unavoidable. Sometimes I wonder whether the worst thing about discovering mogging is becoming conscious of a competition I never even realized I was in.

Mattha Busby is a journalist who covers drug policy, culture, and health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of Energy has issued a seventh “emergency” order forcing J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan to remain open, 534 days after the plant’s planned retirement. The orders have cost ratepayers $303 million and counting, causing electricity prices to increase amid a global energy crisis.

One of the Department of Energy’s recent tactics has been to glitch “emergency orders” forcing coal plants to stay open, even when nobody wants them open.

The DoE has used this on six coal plants (and one oil-and-gas plant) in six states, claiming that the plants need to be kept open for “reliability.”.

According to recent reports, the problem, of course, is that coal is the least reliable form of energy we have available to us. It’s also expensive and polluting, which is why coal use has been plummeting in recent years, dropping from a high of around half of US electricity generation in the early 2000s, down to 17% now.

So everyone is trying to get off coal, for good reason. And when I say “everyone,” I mean everyone – even the owners of the plants subject to these orders have made filings opposing the orders.

The only person trying to keep these coal plants open is fossil shill Chris Wright, posing as head of the Department of Energy, whose main goal is to make American energy supply more expensive and less secure, and ensure that Americans suffer as much harm as possible from it, both to their lungs and pocketbooks.

Each of these orders was obviously illegal from the start – there is no emergency that should force broken coal plants to be reopened, at great cost, in order to sit there idle, providing nothing for ratepayers in the region who are on the hook for the hundreds of millions of dollars that these orders will cost.

Thankfully, courts agreed – even if it took them a while. After more than a year of this nonsense, a federal appeals court blocked these “emergency orders,” specifically targeting the order for the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan. The court unanimously found that there was no emergency keeping it open.

  • The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hospital ratings have become an key resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades revealed the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

It has been revealed that “Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers noted.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers remarked that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

Sources indicate that “Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers mentioned that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

Recent findings suggest that from 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers remarked.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she mentioned.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

Some awards are based on a single procedure, while others are based on a grouping of procedures. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort.
  • Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk.
  • This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, notes Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”.

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

According to recent reports, mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” states Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”.

Recent findings suggest that and just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that my routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

In a recent development, I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

According to recent reports, I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

According to recent reports, heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

In a recent development, by the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

According to recent reports, that mentioned, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

According to recent reports, consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

Recent findings suggest that however, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

Try this 15-minute mobility routine.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”.

Industry observers note that kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

It has been revealed that following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

In a recent development, while there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

Breaking: Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • Industry observers note that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The organization confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a fresh production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

Industry observers note that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

In a recent development, if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we declared a first investment of around € 3b in a latest manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

According to recent reports, per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the upcoming production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla looks to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Sources indicate that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the upcoming hall will be bigger than the original factory.

It has been revealed that the building isn’t newly introduced. Tesla laid out a strategy to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only remarked the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

It has been revealed that giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

Recent findings suggest that so the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

It has been revealed that tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU stated no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

Industry observers note that and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

Recent findings suggest that this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

It has been revealed that good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

BYD is bringing its $10,000 ‘Great’ Seagull overseas, but it won’t replace the Dolphin Surf

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD’s upcoming, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.
  • Industry observers note that the Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China.
  • With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s upcoming, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

Industry observers note that the Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

Industry observers note that in China, the new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

It has been revealed that the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the newly introduced version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The upcoming setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

Recent findings suggest that the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

According to recent reports, in China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

The current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

  • People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease.
  • Industry observers note that both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits.
  • The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Industry observers note that both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study indicates an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Industry observers note that among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she remarked.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea demonstrated a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:.

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.
