Latest Update: How to Do the Walking Lunge for Lower Body Gains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping.
  • In a recent development, enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts.
  • Sources indicate that walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping. So why do most go-to leg exercises have you planting your feet in one spot?

In a recent development, enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts. (A bonus: It’s a unilateral exercise that isn’t the dreaded Bulgarian split squat.) The walking lunge is one of the few strength moves that truly gets you moving. And in doing so, it exposes muscle imbalances, trains balance and coordination, and challenges your core and upper body more than you might expect—all while attacking every muscle in your legs.

Sources indicate that walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before. And in truth, they can be simple. Here, Men’s Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. walks you through the steps to take so that you’re not dragging your feet but making gains toward powerful legs.

FORM IS EVERYTHING with this move. You’ll want to stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, squeeze your glutes and shoulder blades while keeping your gaze at a neutral spot straight ahead of you.

Once you’re comfortable with this slow and controlled movement, you can add weights to build extra muscle and strength. You can hold them at your sides, hold them by your shoulders in what’s called a front rack position, or grab one heavy dumbbell and hold it to your chest in a goblet position. “Regardless of how you hold the load, make sure to keep your upper-body tight,” notes Samuel. “Grip the dumbbells like you mean it, squeeze your shoulder blades, and tighten your abs, too.”.

It has been revealed that don’t obsess over keeping your torso too upright, though, says Samuel. “Especially as you work with heavier loads, don’t be afraid to lean forward slightly,” he says. “That can help you capitalize on your glutes, one of your strongest muscle groups, with each stride.”.

When you’re starting out, says Samuel, aim to take a step that keeps your front shin perpendicular to the ground when you lower your torso into the lunge. But as you grow more experienced, you can play with the length of your stride to chase different goals. “If you take very small steps forward,” says Samuel, “you’ll attack your quads more. Larger steps can help you build hip mobility and knee health. If you take larger steps, go lighter with the load.”.

“The greatest benefits of the walking lunge come from how it challenges us while in motion,” says Samuel. “In addition to building strength and muscle, every step forward challenges your front leg (primarily tibailis and quad muscles) to decelerate your body in space, and then swiftly work to accelerate into the next step. That’s building coordination and balance, in addition to training almost every lower-body muscle and building serious strength.”.

You’ll work a number of major leg muscles when you do walking lunges, including your calves, hamstrings, quads, and glutes.

SMALL MISTAKES IN your walking lunge technique can turn the lower body exercise into a potential knee-wrecking disaster.

Industry observers note that you want to land on the heel of your foot first to provide a strong base for the rest of your lunge position. When you get started with walking lunges, aim for a vertical shin as you lower down to the ground to stay at a 90-degree angle in your front and back legs.

Sources indicate that you also don’t want to think of taking a step forward, but stepping out a couple inches by slightly turning your glute. Another adjustment to protect your knee is to shift your knee slightly outward instead of toward the midline. (If you still feel any knee pain during lunges, try a reverse lunge instead).

In a recent development, keep your torso straight and avoid dipping forward, which you may be more inclined to do if you’re carrying heavy weights for this exercise. Your chest should be aligned with the back of your thigh the entire time. As you get up from the lunge, you want to avoid using momentum. That means no shoulder or torso rocking.

THE WALKING LUNGE is a great way to sneak in some movement on leg day if most of your lower-body exercises have both feet anchored to the ground. Load up some weights, and try to aim for 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg, 1 to 2 times a week. You can alternate each leg or finish up all your reps on one leg before switching to the other. Samuel says that will keep more tension and gives you an opportunity to really focus on the muscle.

According to recent reports, an advantage of this move is its versatility, allowing you to do it anytime, anywhere. If you’re crunched for time or in a hotel room, try bodyweight walking lunges. Do it for 45 seconds with a 15 second rest for 5 minutes to break a sweat and build muscle.

In a recent development, jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

Industry observers note that ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. Before joining Men's Health, he served as a sports columnist and tech columnist for the New York Daily News.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sitting in the leftmost of two left-turn lanes in a latest Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, I notice something strange. I can see my right turn signal on in the reflection of the car in front of me. Then I see my left signal, then my right again. This is less than a mile into an hour testing a new “Level 2++” ADAS system set to be launched by Mercedes, and I have ceded control to what seems to be a hesitant computer that seems to be second-guessing itself.

In a recent development, thankfully, the visible indecision turns into the right choice. The system turns left from the lane, continues on its planned route, and eventually takes a right a quarter-mile later as it had originally intended.

It has been revealed that after the drive, a Mercedes engineer told Road & Track that this could have been a result of disagreement between the priorities of two different systems that go into the MB.Drive-branded point-to-point navigation system. Since the Mercedes ADAS suite uses both the Alpamayo AI model built by Mercedes autonomy partner Nvidia and a “classical stack” of more hard-coded priorities, the engineer inferred that the signal interaction could have been a result of a disagreement between the systems.

The engineer reckoned that the system was trying to think ahead, with the best way to plan for a future right turn being to be in the rightmost of the two left turn lanes. Hence the sudden desire to go one over—a point of conflict. Sometimes, he remarked, the classical path and the end-to-end model end up in conflict. A more cynical take? That our latest robot overlords are already fighting each other.

Sources indicate that the interaction was a particularly odd experience in San Francisco. I work in the city and encounter more advanced self-driving pilot programs from companies like Zoox and Waymo every day. Seeing a Waymo Ojai van in traffic at the same stoplight, I thought about how the “Level 2++” Mercedes system seems to be far off the cutting edge being explored at the global hub of automated taxi development.

It has been revealed that fortunately, that turn-signal confusion never came up again. For the most part, the GLC navigated the busy and often unpredictable streets of San Francisco just before evening rush hour without any need for intervention. I actually deactivated the system just once, to take control the first time I came across a widely parked car in a corner. I otherwise trusted it to figure out everything from jaywalkers to chicanes made of two separate double-parked cars a hundred or so feet apart on opposite sides of a tight road. If I had come across the same parking issue later in the drive, I would have trusted the system without taking over.

Other than the confusion at that first intersection, most of my frustrations with the system came from its combination of cautiousness and aggression. Overly-patient ADAS programming is certainly not a bad thing, but I was regularly met with confusion by motorists at stop signs who wondered why the car took so long to get going after coming to a complete stop.

The system’s decision-making with pedestrians would usually be similarly cautious, as it was when the car slowed for someone waiting for a light to cross well within the bounds of a sidewalk. That person was kicking in the air, something that I inferred the car would pick up as a sign that they might start walking soon, so I let the system make its incorrect guess and slowed from around 35 mph to about 10 mph.

Calculations about pedestrians were not always cautious, though. A few miles later, the system opted to enter an intersection while a slower pedestrian crossed after the light turned green. It came surprisingly close to the pedestrian, still well within a safe distance but nearer than I would have driven personally. This felt a bit unnerving with the car’s high beltline and relatively low visibility over the front fenders, but I never came close enough to have to slam on the brakes and take complete control back.

Recent findings suggest that this is a hands-on system that Mercedes still describes as Level 2 autonomy, even if their 2++ designation obfuscates that fact. It is not true autonomous driving, so I followed the guidelines and kept my hands on the wheel and eyes on the road. The closest comparison is Tesla’s absurdly named Full Self-Driving. When this debuts, Mercedes hopes to be among the first legacy automakers to directly rival the younger EV brands in this space.

Sources indicate that in addition to the headlining point-to-point navigation system, Mercedes allowed us to test a forthcoming hands-free ADAS system available for on-highway use in an S-class and again in a GLE crossover. Unlike the city-driving component, this system allows drivers to completely disengage their hands and feet. It still requires eyes on the road and will aggressively chirp at you to get your hands back on the wheel if you spend too long adjusting a passenger-side mirror. I learned that lesson firsthand, the only time the system forced me to get my eyes back on the road in about 30 miles of highway testing over the two different cars.

This system felt little different from the usual MB.Drive-branded adaptive cruise control. I took control once on this stretch, when the GLE test car signaled to enter a middle lane that a Ram 2500 with a massive trailer was already signaling to enter from the other lane. The system would probably have figured out its own mistake before this became a problem, but I disengaged it entirely and overrode the lane change before I found out how long that would take.

It has been revealed that while both systems are temporarily coming for free to select Mercedes models in California as part of an early-access program in December, final pricing and a nationwide rollout for either system remain to be determined. Hands-free highway assist is planned to reach consumers in spring of next year, available to cars on the MB.OS platform with the existing MB.Drive Assist option package.

Point-to-point navigation, the Tesla-style system for in-city driving, will be available as a subscription model. Mercedes indicates it is coming to cars operating on the brand’s most modern MB.OS-branded architecture starting at some point in 2027. We know that it will be available as a three-year subscription from the factory and in one-year or one-month increments from the car’s digital storefront. Pricing has not been finalized, but a representative from the company claims that it will be “competitive” with comparable offerings from brands like Tesla.

For buyers who prioritize tech that are already looking at one of the products that will be getting the new ADAS suite, the Mercedes system should be worth the eventual subscription price. Given the subscription-only offering and cautious nature of the point-to-point offering, buyers content to drive themselves around a city for a few more years will not be missing out if they opt to forego the new service.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is key since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Sources indicate that subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Industry observers note that both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

Industry observers note that the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He stated it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Recent findings suggest that some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine mentioned.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Recent findings suggest that some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also crucial to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

In a recent development, researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are key for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine remarked, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he mentioned.

Trinh remarked he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#75722. Democracy Depends on Being Able to Forgive

Democracy Depends on Being Able to Forgive

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast this month, President Trump was asked a profound question that rarely comes up in political interviews: Could he forgive his enemies?
  • Recent findings suggest that “The answer is no,” the president said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast this month, President Trump was asked a profound question that rarely comes up in political interviews: Could he forgive his enemies? If entering heaven required him to feel love and forgiveness for James Comey or Nancy Pelosi, could he do it?

Recent findings suggest that “The answer is no,” the president said. “I want to be honest, no.”.

We should resist the tempting thought that only Donald Trump feels this way. We all instead need to look in the mirror: How willing are we to forgive the people we believe have done us wrong?

Sources indicate that for most of us, grievance has a powerful pull—whether it’s rehearsing an argument or replaying a hurtful remark over and over in our heads. In psychology, we can understand forgiveness as a voluntary change in how we feel and act toward someone who’s hurt us in the past. It can loosen the hold of resentment on our attention and, in turn, help us choose how to respond in the future.

In a recent development, these days, the word forgiveness can sound like a concept out of a Sunday school class or a therapy session. But it’s a prerequisite for a functioning democratic society.

A country needs ways to respond to wrongdoing and still leave open the possibility of a shared future. When every injury becomes a reason for retaliation, the work of governing turns into settling scores.

According to recent reports, here’s the thing about democracy: It’s a continuing relationship among fallible people. It depends on our ability to correct errors, acknowledge wrongdoing, and work together again. Forgiveness is a vital civic skill because democratic societies have to do more than settle who was right in the last conflict. Forgiveness makes healthy debate and cooperation possible.

Industry observers note that I once asked the legendary Archbishop Desmond Tutu what forgiveness meant. He simply said, “It means I no longer demand payback from you.”.

Industry observers note that when he was chair of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Tutu helped bring apartheid-era abuses to public attention. He underscored the principle that forgiveness isn’t blanket absolution. Truth, accountability, and repair can coexist with refusing permanent vengeance. In our own lives, we can forgive someone while maintaining boundaries, including choosing not to resume a relationship.

When I interviewed former Colombian president and Nobel Peace laureate Juan Manuel Santos for my book On Belonging, he recalled advice to recognise an adversary’s humanity in war and peace. His 2016 agreement with the FARC opened a path for former guerrillas to enter into democratic politics.

This month, delivering the Nelson Mandela Annual Lecture in South Africa, Santos told the story of Pastora Mira. She cared for a wounded man who then confessed to torturing and killing her son. She embraced him, saying his acceptance of responsibility had freed her from the prison of lifelong hatred. It’s a breathtaking example. Such forgiveness remains a personal choice.

It’s notable that we avoid thinking that the psychological grip of contempt is unique to any one country. Others—including my home country of Canada—shouldn’t think they’re immune to a politics of contempt. A 2025 Angus Reid Institute–Cardus survey found 87% of Conservative supporters regarded the Liberals as a threat to Canada’s well-being. And 84% of Liberal supporters said the same of Conservatives.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt understood forgiveness as a way to release people from being bound indefinitely to what they’ve done, allowing something new to begin. For her, forgiveness was inextricably linked to respect and to what I call belonging—that we honour people’s humanity, even if we disagree with their preferences.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, Texans elected James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, to the U.S. Senate. He’s spoken eloquently about loving his enemies and seeing opponents as children of God. It’s a message that draws on a Christian tradition that asks us to extend the mercy we ourselves need—a tradition Martin Luther King Jr. brought into public life more than half a century ago.

Ultimately, forgiveness is a skill we can learn. In an international study of more than 4,500 adults, people given a short program to reflect on hurt and consider another person’s perspective reported greater forgiveness and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety after two weeks than those waiting to begin. The study concerned personal relationships, but it offers reason to take forgiveness seriously as something we can actively cultivate.

We can all put this into practice. Name what happened and how it honestly affected your feelings. Try to consider the other person’s perspective, and think of a time you needed forgiveness for yourself. Give yourself time and space for your feelings to change. Choosing to forgive can precede feeling the emotion of forgiveness.

Sources indicate that let’s face it: In failing to forgive his enemies, Donald Trump isn’t so much of an outlier. But that needs to change. To build a healthy democratic society, we can’t have permanent enemies. We have to build a future together. That work can begin in our own relationships.

Sources indicate that with seven different back pad positions (from −10 degrees for decline lifts and up to 75 degrees for overhead presses), it packs more multi-functionality than most benches out there. Plus, it has built-in wheels, making it great for home gym spaces that require moving a bench around during workouts to accommodate space.

From Samuel's point of view, this is one of the sturdiest benches he's ever used. "Its tough surface lets me create a great base for bench presses," he notes. An underrated thing he loves: the comfort of the seat portion of the bench, which allows for locking in a good position during overhead presses and incline curls.

It's more expensive than other options in this guide, but if you're looking for a bench that can keep up with your biggest reps and hardest lifts, this pick has got your back.

REP Fitness nailed it with this piece. This is the bench that I choose to lift with at home. The assembly is as easy as you could hope for with a heavy-duty bench like this. A few separate parts connect with screws and an Allen key. Everything was put together and ready for my workout in less than half an hour (just enough time for you to feel accomplished but not tired).

Sources indicate that this bench shines in that it is as comfortable as it is durable. Few benches combine sturdiness, comfort, and versatility like this one from REP Fitness. It offers six different incline angles and a three-post design that anchors it to the floor no matter the exercise. It can also support up to 1,000 pounds, making it a solid option for novice to intermediate lifters.

Industry observers note that "The backrest feels way more cushioned than other benches in its class, yet still manages to deliver rigidity when I drive my shoulder blades down for a set of bench presses," explains Samuel. This bench has only a minimal gap between the seat and back, which has never interfered with any of our lifts. It's also not ridiculously heavy (less than 100 pounds), so it's easy to move around my home gym when needed.

It's also a total breeze to adjust from fully flat up to a 90-degree incline. I've never had an issue with either of the two adjustment mechanisms getting stuck. Three seat positions add to its versatility, too. And the roller pads help secure your lower body with decline sit-ups and decline presses.

Industry observers note that bowflex's flagship 5.1S Collapsible Bench is a good mid-range weight bench for small spaces and beginners. What we love most about this bench is its stowable design—when not in use, it can be stored vertically to reduce its footprint by more than 50 percent. For those who only use a bench at home from time to time and aren't pushing hundreds of pounds per exercise, this transformable option is a great choice.

"This bench is rated to support up to 600 pounds, but keep in mind that it's considerably lightweight," says Samuel. "Meaning if you line up on there for, say, incline rows or preacher curls, it may slip. I find it works best for me for bench presses and seated exercises like press, biceps curls, etc.".

Sources indicate that the position of the leg bar is not perfect, especially for those moving heavy weight, and we found it can act as a roadblock to setting up lifts properly. That being remarked, there is a good number of exercises that you can do properly with this bench not possible with others. It features six adjustable settings, including 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees, flat, and more decline range than most similar benches we've tested (−20 degrees).

Recent findings suggest that flat benches often support more weight than their adjustable counterparts, but the REP Fitness FB-3000 tops the charts with the best weight capacity and comfort features of any flat bench we've tested. Grippy vinyl upholstery prevents slippage on its surface when setting up for a lift, and firm, high-density foam cushioning makes driving down feel as stable as benches double its price. There's even an optional wall hanger for stowing it away when not in use.

It has been revealed that it stands 17 inches from the floor to the top of the pad, and features a three-post design equipped with wheels and a handle to make moving it around easy. Its dimensions are largely consistent with benches used in powerlifting competitions, ensuring powerlifting users a training experience that closely aligns with professional standards. Talk about setting up for success, right?

It has been revealed that "For less than $200, there isn't a better flat bench on the market. Especially for simple, foundational lifts like the bench press," explains Thorp. "I'm a major fan of how simple this bench is, with even padding throughout, making it a solid option for weighted step-ups as well.".

Recent findings suggest that the FB-3000 distinguishes itself with incredible value, but it does come with the same limitations as any flat bench: You miss out on a range of exercises that incline positions on adjustable benches provide. A flat bench is great for most powerlifters, but limiting to the rest of us lifting at home. Beyond its performance, this flat bench comes in various colors, including glossy black, red, blue, and textured versions, allowing users to personalize their gym setup.

Following extensive testing over the years, we've determined this bench to be the most versatile, and a standout in this guide of solid choices, which is why it made our Men’s Health Fitness Awards. This adjustable bench from Prime Fitness USA earned its spot primarily due to its stability—unlike lighter benches, it stays put during exercises on nearly any surface we've tested. Boasting a weight capacity of 1,000 pounds when flat and 600 pounds in an incline position, it can handle substantial weights for various fitness levels.

Seven adjustable backrest positions provide more flexibility than most benches, and the cushioning strikes a perfect balance between comfort and stability. The bench's quick switch between incline settings is also ultra smooth and efficient. Our Fitness Director Samuel enjoys this piece so much he wishes it was an option in the commercial gyms he frequents.

Heavy lifters will love how immovable this bench is: Unlike some lighter benches, it won’t slide away from you with exercises like chest-supported rows—regardless of the surface. With the substantial weight capacity, we felt confident and stable pushing heavy weight on this bench. The trade-off is that it's heavy itself, and while it has built-in wheels for transport, we wouldn't initiative on taking it up and down the stairs a lot.

It has been revealed that the cushioning manages to be comfortable while still providing a stable, sturdy base. Speaking of bases, the footprint on this bench is more sizable than most, so consider dimensions carefully if you're tight on space.

For those in search of a better-looking bench fit for your living room or guest room, this new offering from Matrix is a great option. The build is commercial-grade, and fit for most heavy lifts. This bench is part of a set the manufacturer offers that includes adjustable dumbbells and a storage rack, for those who are seeking a sleek-looking package.

"I like how easy it is to move and store this bench for how stable and sturdy it is," says Thorp. "Combined with the adjustable dumbbells, it brings everything that I need for a solid workout to my basement, with an aesthetic that elevates the room.".

As sturdy as the bench is, it lacks the weight capacity of the Prime or the Hammer Strength benches. Able to handle up to 650 pounds, it should withstand the majority of training scenarios, but if you're a bodybuilder looking to move some real weight, there are probably better places to look in this guide.

The versatility of this bench is another highlight, with five different angles of incline and the ability to reverse the backpad to better support individuals with different body types or other comfort demands. The wheels and handle make it easy to move, and storing against the wall for additional floor space is simple.

This flat bench from Flybird is a suitable option for beginners who are tight on space, offering good value at right around $100. While there are higher-quality flat benches available at a higher price point, the foldable legs make it a standout choice for storage when not in use. The pin and lock system for the folding legs is efficient, taking less than a minute to set up or break down.

The bench is also extremely lightweight, making it easy to move and store as needed. However, for those performing lifts with dumbbells over 50 pounds, a heavier option is preferable for more stability. Despite its lightness, we found it reliable for various exercises like light dumbbell presses, curls, and skullcrushers at home.

Industry observers note that according to Samuel, this is a very solid entry-level bench. "It's more on the cushioned side and actually very comfortable," he explains. "It's obviously not going to do incline and is prone to sliding, so you definitely want a yoga mat under it." It's a budget-friendly option suitable for novice and intermediate lifters, as long as precautions are taken to stabilize the bench.

This bench has become Amazon’s top-selling option because it comes almost fully assembled and seems easy to store. It isn’t the lightest option out there but, for the bench’s advertised versatility, the weight isn’t too bad and it folds up neatly.

We have reservations about this bench though, as it isn’t as stable as it appears—while having a 660-pound capacity, that doesn’t mean you can count on security for all of the movements you might do with it. The padding separation that makes it possible to fold may cause some discomfort when doing decline presses or sit-ups.

Industry observers note that while it won’t be at the top of our recommendations for serious lifters (it will shift on you), it seems to be a decent budget option for beginners who aren’t sure how much they’re going to spend on home gym equipment. Though there is a little added peace of mind coming at the hands of Amazon’s classification, indicating that it’s a product “customers usually keep.”.

First and foremost, you'll need a weight bench strong enough to handle your training regimen—and even if you're not doing heavyweight moves, you'll want it to support a decent amount of load. That's because it's about more than your bodyweight and the weight you're training with; each time you set up on the bench, there's potential for additional impact. In general, aim for a bench that can support at least 500 pounds; that'll set you up for success in nearly all your training and support more advanced exercises that bring even more impact (such as step-ups and plyometric Bulgarians).

The right balance between stiff and cushioned padding is essential to ensure your bench will stay in good condition with use. Highly cushioned benches might feel nice, but they tend to deform over time, creating an uneven surface. This can also compromise your form during workouts, especially when your spine or shoulders are required to stay in alignment. While most padding is stitched to the bench, some is stapled, which tends to lift away from the bench’s frame eventually. Not enough padding isn't good either, as you'll feel like you're lying on a plywood board.

Sources indicate that if you plan on using your adjustable bench for flat bench variations, be mindful of the distance between the back pad and seat pad (otherwise known as the ‘pad gap’). Anything larger than 2 inches will be noticeable and may feel uncomfortable during certain lifts.

In general, the three types of weight benches are flat, adjustable incline, and adjustable incline/decline. The first two are pretty self-explanatory and the latter, of course, adds versatility for decline-angle exercises. "If you're unsure which bench to get, opt for a bench with incline-angle options. Sure, this may cost slightly more initially, but it'll set you up with a bench that can grow with you," explains Samuel. "In general, most website workouts and app workouts assume that, if you're training with a bench, it has incline options. So not having incline options can set you up for frustration. It'll also heavily limit your ability to vary your workouts in fun ways. The incline bench is the most future-proofed purchase option.".

If you're a powerlifter, or you're buying a bench for a particular program, a flat bench might be perfect. Decline-angle benches open up newly introduced movements (especially when it comes to core training), but they're generally unnecessary. Think of that as your luxury option.

According to recent reports, like all home gym equipment, weight benches can take up a lot of room. If you’re tight on space or just appreciate being able to move your equipment out of the way, consider a collapsible weight bench or, at the very least, one with wheels. If you’re after an adjustable weight bench, wheels should be a top priority. Because they’re on the heavier side, this will make stowing away and setting up tremendously easier. You don't want setting up your bench every session to be a part of your workout.

It has been revealed that return policies and warranties represent the manufacturer’s confidence in its product. And with most home gym equipment manufacturers, the better the quality, the better the warranty. In the case that something goes wrong with your bench, it’s important to know your investment is protected, so look for benches that come with at least a one-year warranty.

Industry observers note that as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest training equipment available. I've had extensive experience with weight benches in both the training facilities I've worked out of and the home gyms I've built. I also consulted with Men's Health fitness experts, editors, and writers on the top weight benches they’ve experienced firsthand. The experts included our own Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. The team has tested dozens of weight benches over the years, from high-end, commercial-grade models to budget options.

It has been revealed that our extensive testing process involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors—including size, durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value—to ensure that we recommend only the best. We tested each weight bench through exercise routines that included flat and adjustable bench moves, covering a wide range of motions and use scenarios. To determine stability and structural integrity, we tested benches at both comfortable and near-maximum capacities, allowing us to assess performance under varying loads.

According to recent reports, to gather diverse perspectives, we consulted with our MH Advisory Board and Strength in Diversity trainers, who provided valuable feedback on the top weight benches based on their expertise and experiences. The result is the picks for the best weight benches you can buy right now.

You don’t necessarily need a weight bench to get strong and build muscle, but having one gives you access to a host of exercises (regardless of fitness level), especially when it comes to upper-body training.

It has been revealed that most basic exercises that beginners should master, like dumbbell presses and single-arm dumbbell rows and hip thrusts, are much easier to execute with a bench (especially an adjustable one). Meanwhile, more advanced lifters can get incredible mileage out of a bench by unlocking more innovative moves like half-bench single-arm presses and single-arm rows.

Here's a breakdown of the key differences:.

A flat weight bench is designed with a fixed, flat surface, whereas an adjustable weight bench allows you to adjust the angle of the bench to different incline or, in some cases, decline angles.

"The adjustable benches that offer a decline setting are a terrific value for anyone who wants to get creative with their core exercises while training at home," claims Samuel.

"Adjustable benches give you so many more options for your exercises," explains David Otey, C.S.C.S and Men's Health Advisory Board member. "Instead of just working at flat or upright, all of the angles in between can give you variety and diversity in your training options." Those angles allow you to bias muscle groups in different, more selective ways. A flat weight bench limits you to exercises that can be performed on a flat surface.

Industry observers note that adjustable benches offer more convenience overall (especially well-built ones), offering access to more movements and angles. Adjustable benches also offer support for extra movements, such as overhead presses and lateral raises, which can allow for greater loading of those movements in the long term. But flat weight benches win for convenience in two areas. They're generally lighter, so you can more easily move them around your gym, and they're easier to stow when not in use, too.

Because flat weight benches generally have fewer mechanisms and lack a hinge of any sort, they'll be easier to maintain. Adjustable benches don't require a ton of maintenance, but it's worthwhile every so often to check on bolts and caps, and make sure your hinge mechanism is working smoothly.

We consulted with Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., for the best exercises for beginners to get the most out of a weight bench.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Mercedes-Benz Is Bringing Tesla-Like Semi-Autonomous Driving Systems to America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (427 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States.
  • The hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use.
  • In a recent development, while both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States. That system is no longer available in the latest revision to the S-Class, with CTO Jörg Burzer calling it “early.” The brand still has advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) ambitions, though, and two newly introduced major products are arriving for a few customers starting next year. Mercedes-Benz has declared plans to launch both hands-free highway driving and hands-on point-to-point navigation in 2027, part of a continuing partnership with (scandal-laden) semiconductor superpower Nvidia. The latter system is subscription-only, although pricing for that subscription has yet to be revealed.

The hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use. It works up to 85 miles per hour, allowing a driver to take their hands off all inputs while the system handles highway driving and decision-making under the driver’s active supervision. Point-to-point navigation, on the other hand, is a hands-on system with more freedom. Like Tesla or Rivian’s similar offerings, it is intended to handle most of the workload of city driving and react in real time to the peculiarities of that task.

In a recent development, while both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy. That label means that they are meant to be seen as driver assistance systems only, leaving the person in the driver’s seat ultimately responsible for intervening before a problem occurs. The same is true of every autonomous solution currently on offer, including systems marketed as “Full Self-Driving” by Tesla.

It has been revealed that some California residents will receive the opportunity to try both systems starting in December; hands-free driving is expected to reach eligible cars more broadly in spring of 2027, while point-to-point navigation is made available nationwide at some point during the next year. Subscription pricing has not yet been declared, but brand representatives have suggested to Road & Track that it will be “competitive” with similar offerings from other automakers.

It has been revealed that mercedes allowed outlets, including Road & Track, to test both systems in San Francisco ahead of the news. You can read more about how the new ADAS offerings fared here.

Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

#75719. Tech Report: Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

Tech Report: Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause.
  • Cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle.
  • These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”.

Cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

Recent findings suggest that but within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, says Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have substantial implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

In a recent development, the lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

There’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

It has been revealed that menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” indicates Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in Newly introduced York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

Recent findings suggest that when doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” states Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care tech giant Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

Industry observers note that tikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

In a recent development, milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she notes. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

Sources indicate that for instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she states. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”.

For daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” says Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at Mission Connection.

Even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she says. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”.

Having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard says. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

Industry observers note that in fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck says. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Recent findings suggest that even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) issue still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio says. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”.

Mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, indicates Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

On the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she says. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”.

According to recent reports, cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she indicates.

Even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

#75716. Egg Donation: Is It Private, or a Secret?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1080 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Egg Donation: Is It Private, or a Secret?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • When it comes to donor conception, there is an key difference between protecting your privacy and keeping a secret.
  • Industry observers note that A woman I was working with recently voiced that her biggest concern about using an egg donor was disclosure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

When it comes to donor conception, there is an key difference between protecting your privacy and keeping a secret.

Industry observers note that A woman I was working with recently voiced that her biggest concern about using an egg donor was disclosure. She worried about how certain family members might react. She anticipated judgment, unwanted opinions, and criticism.

She wasn't questioning whether egg donation was right for her. Rather, she was questioning who needed to know and whether that knowledge could come back to hurt her or her family.

Sources indicate that our work raised two notable questions: Whose information is it to share? And what is the difference between privacy and secrecy?

These terms are often used interchangeably, but privacy and secrecy are not necessarily the same thing.

It has been revealed that privacy is about choosing what information to share, with whom and when. Secrecy, on the other hand, often involves deliberately withholding information, sometimes because of shame, fear, or anticipated judgment.

Take, for example, a woman who decides not to tell her mother-in-law that she used an egg donor. Perhaps their relationship is difficult. Perhaps she knows her mother-in-law has strong opinions about what makes a family.

Naturally, she may worry that her child will be treated or seen differently. And alongside this may be a concern that her own place as a mother will somehow be questioned.

Does that mean she is keeping a secret? Perhaps. But it may also be about privacy. She may simply be sparing herself from a conversation she doesn't want or need to have. This is personal information that belongs to her, her partner and their child. It is not necessarily something the wider family needs to know.

But she may also feel that she has no choice but to hide the information because she fears how her mother-in-law might react.

Industry observers note that this is where privacy and secrecy can overlap. She may want to keep the information private, while also feeling that she cannot safely share it. Both can be true at the same time.

And keeping something secret does not automatically mean that someone feels ashamed or that their decision is wrong.

While parents have every right to decide who knows about their fertility treatment, donor conception also involves another person: the child. And the child's relationship with this information is different. For the child, it is part of the story of how they came into the world.

Research supports telling donor-conceived children about their origins early, using age-appropriate language and making it part of their developing understanding of themselves, rather than a “one and done” significant conversation when the child is older (Ilioi et al., 2017; Duff & Goedeke, 2024). There can be something deeply reassuring about growing up with this knowledge, rather than having to make sense of it for the first time later in life.

As the child grows, the conversation also grows. Questions change, newly introduced feelings emerge, and things that seemed unimportant at five may take on a different meaning at fifteen.

But what happens when parents tell their child about their conception and then ask them not to tell anyone else?

Parents may have understandable reasons for wanting to keep donor conception within the immediate family. They may want to protect their child from judgment, insensitive comments, or rejection.

But imagine a child who has always known they were conceived through egg donation, yet has been told not to mention it to grandparents or friends.

Perhaps a friend asks why they don't look like their mother. The child may want to explain but hesitate, remembering that their parents don't want anyone to know. In this way they are caught between wanting to talk about themselves and worrying about upsetting their parents.

A child may also begin to wonder: Why can we talk about this at home but not outside? Is there something wrong with how I was conceived? This is where privacy may begin to feel like secrecy. Privacy gives a child a choice about what they share, while secrecy may leave them feeling responsible for keeping something hidden.

As children grow older, they develop their own feelings about their genetic origins. Some may want to talk openly about being donor-conceived, others may prefer privacy. What matters is that the child is gradually given the language, understanding and freedom to decide what they feel comfortable sharing.

For example, they might say, “My parents needed help from an egg donor to have me.”.

Or equally, “I don't really want to talk about that.”.

Both are reasonable responses. The notable difference is that the choice belongs to them.

Sources indicate that it is OK for parents and children to have different feelings about disclosure. What is important is that parents recognize their own anxieties and try not to pass them on to their child. The child should feel free to develop their own feelings about their origins, without carrying the weight of their parents' worries.

This can be a complex challenge for parents to come to terms with. And it doesn't have to be neatly resolved. It can just be.

Not everyone will understand or approve. Some may have deeply held beliefs about genetics and family relationships. Others may ask intrusive questions or make insensitive comments. You cannot necessarily prevent those reactions, but you can decide how much access those individuals have to your private lives.

In a recent development, depending on your family and community, it may also be vital to prepare your child for the fact that people have different ideas about what makes a family. Not everyone will agree with your views, and they don't have to. This too is part of diversity. There are many different ways to be human.

According to recent reports, duff, M. A., & Goedeke, S. (2024). Parents' disclosure to their donor-conceived children in the last 10 years and factors affecting disclosure: A narrative review. Human Reproduction Patch, 30(4), 488–527. doi.org/10.1093/humupd/dmae010.

Ilioi, E. C., Blake, L., Jadva, V., Roman, G., & Golombok, S. (2017). The role of age of disclosure of biological origins in the psychological wellbeing of adolescents conceived by reproductive donation: A longitudinal study from age 1 to age 14. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 58(3), 315–324. doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.12667.

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data indicates a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Recent findings suggest that tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

According to recent reports, across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

According to recent reports, in the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Sources indicate that engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

Industry observers note that what the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

Sources indicate that to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

BMW just unearthed something exceedingly cool from its cellars, something that we never even knew existed: a BMW M7 Prototype.

In a recent development, revealed via a post on BMW Classic’s Instagram and brought to broader attention to BMWBlog, the video gives us our first look ever at this performance sedan that never was. Conceived in the late 1990s, this 7-Series started life out as a 1997 BMW 740i; BMW then swapped in the 4.9-liter naturally aspirated V-8 from the E39 M5, imbuing it with 400 horsepower.

Not only does it have the M5’s engine, but BMW also paired the motor with a six-speed manual transmission. BMW says the M7 Prototype has a top speed of 155 mph and weighs 4134 pounds. Unfortunately, that’s when the details begin to fall off, and we’re left to observe—or guess—any other info.

Being an M7 Prototype, we suspect BMW went all-out in its M endeavors. That would mean a far sportier chassis alongside larger wheels and tires. This prototype is fitted with BBS wheels, giving it a notably more aggressive stance and look than your typical 740i. The car’s design itself remains understated, making sure to maintain its 7-Series elegance; that mentioned, the rear bumper is modified to make room for the quad exhaust tips you’d see poking out the rear of the E39 M5. No 7-Series from this era featured such an outwardly aggressive exhaust exit, making it one of the few standout exterior changes to this car.

In a recent development, BMW also upholstered the interior with a classy tan and black two-tone. The six-speed shifter is integrated cleanly with the center console. It has a three-spoke M steering wheel, and the cluster is an M unit borrowed from the E39 M5 as well. Suffice it to say, we’re a little sad the firm never brought this to production.

Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you.
  • “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” claims sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open.
  • Sources indicate that you also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research shows that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” claims sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”.

Sources indicate that you also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin notes.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Sources indicate that even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

It has been revealed that when you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin claims. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin indicates. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is crucial as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

According to recent reports, studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin states. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.
